chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdullah, from Al-Hasan ibn Mahboub, from Malik ibn Atiyya, from Aamir ibn Juza'ah, who said:

A man came to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) and said to him, 'O Abu Abdullah, give me a loan to be repaid when I am financially ease.' So Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) said to him, 'Until you realize a harvest?' The man said, 'No, by Allah.' He (peace be upon him) said, 'Then until your profit in a trade?' He said, 'No, by Allah.' He (peace be upon him) said, 'Then until a contract is fulfilled?' He said, 'No, by Allah.'

So Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) said, 'Thus, you are from those for whom Allah has made a right in our wealth.' Then he called for a bag containing dirhams, inserted his hand into it, and handed him a handful. Then he said to him, 'Fear Allah and do not be extravagant nor stingy, but be upright in between. Indeed, squandering is from extravagance.'
Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: 'And do not squander wastefully.'
Al-Hasan ibn Mahboub, from Sa'dan ibn Muslim, from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) — similar to that.
ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ethical stance on loans and financial balance between extravagance and stinginess?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Kafi elucidates the jurisprudential criteria for lending from the Imam's treasury, distinguishing between loans for productive trade ('tijarah') and those for mere speculation or debt repayment. It further establishes the ethical principle of 'Qawam' (balanced moderation) in spending, warning against both Israf (extravagance) and Qutr (stinginess), thereby linking financial prudence to spiritual balance.
